notes.summary: On 21 October Microsoft Threat Intelligence published its analysis of a large, AI-automated campaign by Storm-0940, which it describes as a China-state aligned actor active since 2021, using the open-source ARTEX penetration-testing framework. Microsoft says it assesses that Storm-0940 was responsible for the ConnectWise supply-chain compromise of the multi-tenant Cloud Backup application, and that the actor reached privileged cloud access in some cases less than three hours after first targeting. After taking control of ConnectWise application identities, the actor signed in to more than 2,250 downstream tenants through applications those customers had already trusted, and in some tenants moved on to Graph reconnaissance, credential additions to applications and privileged role changes, including one application that gave itself Global Administrator. Microsoft states this was not caused by a vulnerability in or compromise of Microsoft systems, and that a sign-in does not by itself prove data was accessed. The page does not say how the ConnectWise identities were first compromised.

timeline.text: Password-spray campaign starts from 144.172.64[.]99 against 327 accounts in eight organizations (10-14 Oct); about 151,000 failed logons, peak 2,900 failures per minute on 11 Oct.
Public reports of the ConnectWise compromise appear, citing IOCs in the same network range.
ConnectWise publishes an initial advisory, later expanded; one of its IPs matches 144.172.64[.]99.
Microsoft publishes the attribution and the hunting and detection guidance.

notes.rootCause: Microsoft names no software vulnerability. The contributing factors it lists are compromised multi-tenant application identities holding high privileges, the trust and consent customers had already granted to those applications, password spraying against Microsoft 365 accounts, and machine-speed automation. It does not describe how the ConnectWise identities were initially compromised.
attacker: Used ARTEX, a multi-agent LLM framework that can run autonomous tests from reconnaissance to data exfiltration, to speed up targeting.
Ran a cross-tenant password spray against Microsoft 365 and Exchange Online (10-14 Oct).
Took control of identities of several ConnectWise cloud applications and used them to authenticate to customer tenants without interactive user sign-in (about 2,900 attempts per minute).

In some tenants: Graph and directory reconnaissance, application credential changes for persistence, changes to identities, groups and privileged roles; one application self-assigned Global Administrator (T1098.003).
Microsoft notes that backdoor credentials added to applications can survive remediation of the compromised application.
iocs: IP 144.172.64[.]128 (app sign-ins and Graph activity)
IP 144.172.64[.]99 (password spray; matches a ConnectWise advisory IP)
IP 144.172.64[.]60 (sign-ins and Graph activity)
User agents Python-urllib/3.12, python-requests/2.31.0, python-requests/2.34.2, curl/7.88.1, azure-toolkit/1.0
ConnectWise application IDs 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae (Cloud Backup), 24205314-2b89-4e07-a2a4-579e898a5640 (MS Teams), 0de14c77-b9b0-4137-9360-34878a929827 (MS Graph)

remediation.text: Keep the affected ConnectWise application connections disabled until ConnectWise gives formal restoration instructions; do not delete the enterprise applications first, preserve configuration and evidence.
Inventory the application IDs above and record the local service principal object IDs in each tenant; search by application ID, not display name.

Preserve Entra sign-in and audit logs, Purview Audit records and Graph telemetry; review service-principal sign-ins from at least 15 Oct, extended to 1 Oct, successes and failures separately and not only the published IPs.

Review Entra audit records for credential additions, new apps, service principals or owners, app-role assignments, consent grants, privileged role assignments and changes to authentication methods or Conditional Access; review mailbox forwarding, inbox and transport rules and delegate permissions.
After preserving evidence, have an authorized responder remove confirmed unauthorized credentials, grants, owners, assignments and identities, revoke unneeded permissions and rotate credentials.
Apply least privilege to multi-tenant application permissions and consent grants; alert on credential additions, privileged role assignment and anomalous app-only activity.
An empty hunting result is not proof of no access: Microsoft says so explicitly, so check the audit trail as well.

stories.appsNote: Older tenants may list the Cloud Management applications as "SkyKick Cloud Manager". Search by application ID, not by name. Owner tenant of the vendor's applications (an indicator on service-principal events): 3f9cd7a0-127a-4ed4-bf06-2f830d5616b7 (Huntress).

notes.summary: An attacker used the shared credential of ConnectWise Cloud Backup's multi-tenant Entra application (formerly SkyKick) to sign in as the app in customer tenants. Because the sign-in was an app (client credentials) sign-in from a script, user MFA and user Conditional Access did not apply. In about 50 tenants the vendor's 'Cloud Management' service principals assigned themselves directory roles, mostly Exchange Administrator, and in at least one tenant Global Administrator, then added client secrets to other applications for persistence. ConnectWise says it found the activity on 14 October, disabled seven app identities on 17 October and invalidated the shared credentials on 18 October; its root-cause analysis was still open on 19 October.

timeline.text: Password spray from 144.172.64[.]128 against four law-firm tenants (13-14 Oct).
ConnectWise detects the activity (its own statement).

01:58 UTC: Cloud Management service principals start assigning themselves directory roles (mostly Exchange Administrator) in about 50 tenants; 06:13-08:34 UTC the backup app obtains Graph tokens tenant by tenant; a second, manual-looking wave follows.
Huntress publishes: 162 affected tenants (173 later). Sign-in attempts in about 1,000 tenants, about 300 successful (The Hacker News).

ConnectWise disables 7 application identities at 07:00 UTC and revokes their certificates; SpecterOps publishes a tenant check; Microsoft Threat Intelligence posts on X about an active supply-chain attack on a trusted OAuth app.
ConnectWise: the shared Cloud Backup credentials are no longer valid; no sign backup data was compromised. Cloud Backup suspended.

notes.rootCause: One credential (client assertion / API secret) shared by the vendor's multi-tenant application across every customer tenant that had consented to it. Whoever held it could act as the app in all of them, with the application permissions the customers had granted (Directory.ReadWrite.All is named by Microsoft as likely abused) and the directory roles it could assign to itself.
attacker: Signed in as the vendor's service principals with client credentials (scripted: Python-urllib/3.12, python-requests, curl/7.88.1).
Assigned directory roles to the vendor's service principals (Exchange Administrator; Global Administrator in one tenant).
Added client secrets valid until 2028 to other applications in the tenant (an MSP management app, a security vendor's app) for persistence.
Graph API reconnaissance; with Exchange Administrator, access to mailbox configuration (forwarding, inbox rules).
iocs: IP 144.172.64[.]128 (password spray and app sign-ins)
User agents Python-urllib/3.12, python-requests/2.31 and 2.34.2, curl/7.88.1 on service-principal sign-ins
Service principals named ConnectWise Cloud Backup, Cloud Management (Exchange / Teams / SharePoint), SkyKick Cloud Manager in older tenants
Audit events 'Add member to role', 'Update application', 'Add service principal credentials' initiated by an application after 13 Oct 2026

remediation.text: Disable (do not delete) every ConnectWise / SkyKick enterprise application in the tenant - the seven application IDs are listed under Applications involved: Entra admin center > Enterprise applications > the app > Properties > Enabled for users to sign in = No. Deleting removes the consent and the evidence.
Remove any directory role the vendor's service principals hold (Roles and administrators > filter by the app) and check PIM for eligible assignments.
Do not re-enable the ConnectWise applications until ConnectWise confirms all of their credentials were reset. Disabling pauses backups - confirm retention and restore options with ConnectWise.

Review every credential added to any application or service principal since 13 Oct 2026 (Audit logs: 'Add service principal credentials', 'Update application - Certificates and secrets management') and remove the ones nobody in your team added.
Review service-principal sign-ins of the vendor's apps (Sign-in logs > Service principal sign-ins) for the IP and user agents above.
Check mailbox forwarding, inbox rules, federation trusts (domain federation settings) and new consent grants.
Check Conditional Access for policies that exclude these applications from location-based blocks.
Existing tokens stay valid for up to 90 minutes after an app is disabled - repeat the checks after that window.
Turn on Microsoft Graph activity logs (diagnostic setting MicrosoftGraphActivityLogs) so the next app-only access is visible request by request.

Inventory every multi-tenant third-party app with application permissions that can write the directory (Directory.ReadWrite.All, RoleManagement.ReadWrite.Directory, AppRoleAssignment.ReadWrite.All, Application.ReadWrite.All) - each one is the same single point of failure; use the Graph API tab of this portal to see what each permission allows.
Apply an app management policy that blocks new password credentials (client secrets) on applications, and Conditional Access for workload identities (location / risk) on the vendor apps you keep.
Alert on a service principal adding itself or another service principal to a directory role, and on a credential added to an application by an application (KQL below).

kql.title: Role assignments made by applications (Sentinel / Defender: AuditLogs)
kql.query:
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > datetime(2026-10-13)
| where OperationName == "Add member to role"
| where isnotempty(tostring(InitiatedBy.app.servicePrincipalId))
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.app.displayName),
         Role = tostring(TargetResources[0].modifiedProperties[1].newValue),
         Target = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName)
| project TimeGenerated, Actor, Target, Role, CorrelationId

kql.title: Credentials added to applications or service principals
kql.query:
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > datetime(2026-10-13)
| where OperationName has_any ("Add service principal credentials", "Certificates and secrets management")
| extend Actor = coalesce(tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), tostring(InitiatedBy.app.displayName)),
         App = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Actor, App, Result

kql.title: Service-principal sign-ins from the reported IP or scripted user agents
kql.query:
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > datetime(2026-10-13)
| where IPAddress == "144.172.64.128"
    or ServicePrincipalName has_any ("ConnectWise", "SkyKick", "Cloud Management")
| summarize SignIns = count(), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20), First = min(TimeGenerated), Last = max(TimeGenerated)
    by ServicePrincipalName, AppId, ResultType

stories.title: Beyond source code: a self-service password reset on one account led to Azure DevOps pipelines and Kubernetes credentials

items.title: ​​Beyond source code: A path to the keys to the kingdom

microsoft.checked: Microsoft Threat Intelligence, Microsoft Security Blog, Microsoft Incident Response, MSRC Security Update Guide, Message Center (mc.merill.net, 60 days)

notes.summary: Microsoft's Detection and Response Team described an intrusion that began with a single user account taken over through self-service password reset (SSPR). The attacker registered their own authentication methods, then used legitimate admin tools and scripts to enumerate Azure DevOps repositories, projects and pipelines. A malicious pipeline harvested Kubernetes credentials (kubeconfig files); pipeline scripts were then changed to install the Atera remote management agent and the Chisel tunnelling tool. The page attributes the activity to Storm-3068 and gives no attack dates and no IOC values. The case shows how an identity weakness spreads when development platforms, pipelines and cloud infrastructure are tightly connected.

timeline.text: Microsoft publishes the incident-response write-up; the page gives no dates for the intrusion itself.

notes.rootCause: Initial access was abuse of self-service password reset on a user account, followed by registration of attacker-controlled authentication methods. The impact grew because the account's permissions reached Azure DevOps pipelines authorised for more than 50 resources. The page does not state a formal root cause.
attacker: Took over a user account through self-service password reset and registered their own authentication methods.
Enumerated Azure DevOps repositories, projects, pipelines and deployment environments with legitimate tools and scripts.
Created a pipeline that deployed a kube agent and collected kubeconfig files at scale.
Modified pipeline scripts to install the Atera agent and download the Chisel tunnelling utility; Chisel opened a reverse tunnel to an external IP address (value not published).
Committed seven stolen kubeconfig files to a repository.

remediation.text: Monitor password reset activity for unusual patterns, such as repeated attempts or activity across multiple users.
Limit privileged accounts' exposure to self-service password reset and require phishing-resistant MFA.
Require approvals for code changes, enforce branch protection and restrict direct commits to critical branches.
Control who can create, modify or run build and deployment pipelines; apply least privilege across identities, development platforms and cloud resources.
Review recently registered authentication methods on accounts that completed a password reset, and review Azure DevOps audit logs for new or changed pipelines.

stories.title: Storm-3168 (JADEPUFFER): agentic destructive attack in Azure through compromised service principals

items.title: Storm-3168: Agentic-driven cloud attacks using compromised service principals

microsoft.checked: Microsoft Threat Intelligence, Microsoft Security Blog, Microsoft Incident Response, MSRC Security Update Guide, Message Center (mc.merill.net, 60 days)

notes.summary: Microsoft investigated malicious Azure activity in one compromised tenant where two service principals were used: one for reconnaissance, the other for discovery, bulk deletion and credential collection. More than 150 destructive or credential-collection operations ran over 35 minutes, hitting storage accounts, a Key Vault, a Function App and an App Service plan; SQL deletions failed on an unsupported API version and some deletions were stopped by resource locks. Microsoft saw no ransom note and did not confirm data exfiltration. The actor is tracked as Storm-3168 and is associated with JADEPUFFER, which Sysdig reported in July 2026 as the first documented agentic ransomware operation.

timeline.text: Early June: the first service principal enumerates VMs, subscriptions and resources for about 15.5 hours; the second follows about 90 minutes later and later enumerates App Service configuration stores. (Microsoft gives the month only; the 1st is a placeholder.)
Sysdig discovers JADEPUFFER (as reported by Microsoft). (Microsoft gives the month only; the 1st is a placeholder.)
Microsoft Security Research publishes the analysis.

notes.rootCause: Initial access is unconfirmed. Microsoft found a client ID, secret and tenant ID posted in plaintext in a public GitHub issue by an employee and still visible in the edit history, but could not confirm that credential was used. The service principals held broad Azure RBAC roles (Contributor, Storage Account Contributor, SQL DB Contributor), which made the deletions possible.
attacker: Used existing Azure RBAC assignments of the two service principals; five unique tokens for the destructive principal, two active in the same 70-second window, assessed as automated.
User agent python-requests/2.34.2 and shared infrastructure for both principals.
Tried to delete Azure Site Recovery and Azure Backup protection locks (failed), then listed storage account keys 30+ times after the destruction.
iocs: 45.131.66[.]106 (App Service probing and malicious ARM requests)
34.153.223[.]102 (App Service probing)
64.20.53[.]230 (App Service probing)
User agent python-requests/2.34.2

remediation.text: Treat publicly exposed credentials as compromised even after the source is edited: rotate immediately and review historical use.
Apply least privilege to service principals through Azure RBAC and prefer mechanisms that reduce long-lived credentials.
Use resource locks and deletion protection, restrict access to backup and recovery resources and monitor attempts to change their protection.
Enable the Defender for Cloud plans for Resource Manager, Storage, Key Vault, App Service and Databases.

stories.title: Sideloaded AppX package abuses Microsoft-signed web hosts to capture OAuth tokens (Huntress research)

microsoft.checked: Microsoft Threat Intelligence, Microsoft Security Blog, Microsoft Incident Response, MSRC Security Update Guide, Message Center (mc.merill.net, 60 days)

notes.summary: Huntress researcher Andrew Schwartz showed that a sideloaded AppX package can use Microsoft-signed AppX web hosts such as WWAHost.exe to show a genuine Microsoft sign-in, complete MFA and hand the authorization code to attacker JavaScript, which exchanges it for access and refresh tokens. It is post-compromise: it needs code execution in the user's session and Developer Mode or an enterprise sideloading policy. It was proven end to end on Windows 11 24H2 against a test tenant with MFA. Huntress names no threat actor and discloses no attacker infrastructure, so this is a technique, not an observed campaign. The Entra sign-in looks like a normal Office sign-in with no risk flags.

timeline.text: Huntress publishes the research; the page gives no date for the testing itself.

notes.rootCause: A design issue in the shared WinRT activation layer: a sideloaded package with WindowsRuntimeAccess="all" in ContentUriRules gives remote JavaScript the WinRT surface, with no caller validation, and the legacy WebAuthenticationBroker is reachable from inside the host. Developer Mode or the AllowAllTrustedApps policy is the gating condition.
attacker: Registers a package with Add-AppxPackage -Register as a standard user; the manifest points ContentUriRules at an attacker server.
Calls WebAuthenticationBroker.authenticateAsync() with Microsoft Office's first-party client ID and the urn:ietf:wg:oauth:2.0:oob redirect URI.
The user sees a real Microsoft login with no address bar and completes MFA.
Receives the authorization code through the broker callback, exchanges it and exfiltrates the access and refresh tokens.
iocs: User agent MSAppHost/3.0 (Edge/18) reaching non-Microsoft destinations (broker leg: MSAuthHost/1.0)
AppXDeploymentServer/Operational Event ID 400 (successful register)
Add-AppxPackage -Register from paths outside C:\Program Files\WindowsApps

remediation.text: Deploy the Sigma proxy rule on user agent MSAppHost/3.0 with a Microsoft domain allow-list tuned to your environment.
Audit Developer Mode across the fleet and disable 'Allow all trusted apps to install' by GPO.
Require compliant or managed devices for token issuance with Conditional Access and pair with Token Protection where available.
Shorten refresh-token lifetimes and enable Continuous Access Evaluation.

links.text: OAuth Token Theft Through Microsoft's Front Door

stories.title: EvilTokens: a phishing-as-a-service kit that steals Microsoft 365 tokens through device code phishing

items.title: Unmasking EvilTokens: Getting to the root of device code phishing

microsoft.checked: Microsoft Threat Intelligence, Microsoft Security Blog, Microsoft Incident Response, MSRC Security Update Guide, Message Center (mc.merill.net, 60 days)

notes.summary: EvilTokens is a phishing-as-a-service platform that appeared in February 2026 and abuses the OAuth device code flow. Microsoft says its campaigns compromised more than 12,000 inboxes in over 10,000 organizations. The victim is shown a real device code and sent to the genuine microsoft.com/devicelogin page, so the sign-in and MFA are done by the victim and the attacker receives the tokens without ever seeing a password. Stolen tokens were used to read and exfiltrate mail, create inbox rules and in some cases register a device to obtain a Primary Refresh Token. Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit coordinated a disruption of the infrastructure.

timeline.text: EvilTokens emerges as a phishing-as-a-service platform sold through Telegram. (Microsoft gives the month only; the 1st is a placeholder.)
Microsoft tracks a related campaign that used automation platforms to start short-lived polling nodes running Node.js backend logic. (Microsoft gives the month only; the 1st is a placeholder.)
Microsoft Threat Intelligence publishes its analysis and describes the coordinated disruption by the Digital Crimes Unit.

notes.rootCause: The device code flow lets a third party start a sign-in that the victim completes on a legitimate Microsoft page. Where Conditional Access does not block the flow, the attacker's polling script receives valid tokens after the victim signs in with MFA.
attacker: Developer and operator of the kit is tracked as Storm-2992; sold on Telegram for $1,500 plus $500 per month.

Lures by email (invoices, RFPs, shared files, password-expiry notices) with URLs, PDF or HTML attachments, behind fake CAPTCHA pages and multi-stage redirects on Vercel, Cloudflare Workers and AWS Lambda.
A background script requests a live device code, shows it with Copy Code and Continue buttons and polls the actor's /state endpoint every three to five seconds for up to 15 minutes.

After sign-in: Microsoft Graph reconnaissance, AI-assisted search for financial and executive mailboxes, wire-transfer and invoice keywords, malicious inbox rules, and device registration to obtain a Primary Refresh Token within about 10 minutes.
iocs: Hosting abused: .vercel.app, .workers.dev, AWS Lambda (named by Microsoft)
Legitimate page abused: microsoft.com/devicelogin
Microsoft lists no IP addresses or file hashes in this post

remediation.text: Block the device code flow with Conditional Access wherever possible; where Teams devices need it, scope the exception to the Teams device resource accounts and exclude the Device Registration Service resource.
Revoke refresh tokens with revokeSignInSessions for a suspected account and consider disabling it temporarily; access tokens can stay valid for up to an hour.
Require phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO, Authenticator with passkeys), enable sign-in risk policies and Continuous Access Evaluation, block legacy authentication.
Configure anti-phishing, Safe Links and ZAP, raise the Advanced Phishing Threshold to 2 or 3 and alert on suspicious inbox rule creation.
